1.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will raise up against Babylon, and against them that dwell in the midst of them that rise up against me, a destroying wind; And will send unto Babylon fanners, that shall fan her, and shall empty her land: for in the day of trouble they shall be against her round about.

schools.summary: Work the philology: the wind of a destroyer, and the letter-cipher that resolves the last clause into the name of the Chaldeans.
Read the chapter as the enlargement of the last, and defend the prophet's length on the ground that an incredible event needed many figures.
Set out the whole argument in advance and mark the sublimity of the figures, describing the threshing-floor behind the fanners.
Warns that the chapter resists division, its particulars dispersed and interwoven and to be gathered under heads.

debates.question: Is the destroying wind literal or figurative?

positions.position: Literally the wind of a destroyer, though the same phrase is used elsewhere of stirring up a man's spirit; the fanners of the next verse pull toward the plain meaning.
A similitude, and a very appropriate one, since it reminds men how easily God could destroy the world by a single blast, and sets his power against the elaborate preparations of human war.

debates.question: Does the word behind fanners mean strangers or winnowers?

positions.position: Strangers as it stands; a change of pointing would give winnowers, a form found nowhere else, so the prophet set the noun beside the verb for assonance.
Either will do, the agents being the Medes and Persians, a strong wind on the threshing mountains.
Aliens is a harsh sense; the allusion to the wind already mentioned should be kept.

outliers.claim: Identifies the last clause as the Atbash cipher, resolving into the name of the Chaldeans, and argues the cipher-words had become familiar in correspondence between the exiles and those left in Judaea, so both parties would understand them.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will raise up against Babylon, and against them that dwell in the midst of them that rise up against me, a destroying wind;
And will send unto Babylon fanners, that shall fan her, and shall empty her land: for in the day of trouble they shall be against her round about.

3.pericope_label: Against him that bendeth let the archer bend his bow, and against him that lifteth himself up in his brigandine: and spare ye not her young men; destroy ye utterly all her host. Thus the slain shall fall in the land of the Chaldeans, and they that are thrust through in her streets. For Israel hath not been forsaken, nor Judah of his God, of the Lord of hosts; though their land was filled with sin against the Holy One of Israel. Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and deliver every man his soul: be not cut off in her iniquity; for this is the time of the Lord’s vengeance; he will render unto her a recompence.

schools.summary: Press the grammar of the archers and the disputed preposition of the flight, and correct forsaken to widowed.
Take the widowhood as a temporary divorce from a marriage-bond that holds, and read the doubled slaughter as reaching field and city alike.
Read the verse of prophets still sent in the midst of deserved punishment, and propose that the word rendered sin means punishment.

debates.question: What does it mean that Israel has not been forsaken?

positions.position: Better, not widowed; Judah and Israel were not abandoned by their husband, and the assurance rests on no plea in extenuation of the guilt the next words admit.
The exile looked like a repudiation and they were for a time like widows, but the divorce was temporary, the church having been joined to God as by a marriage-bond.
God continued his prophets among them and remembered mercy in the midst of wrath; the word rendered sin here rather means punishment.
Not utterly forsaken.

debates.question: Who is told to flee, and in what sense?

positions.position: Either foreigners there on business or the captive Jews, with an application to the mystical city.
The call reproduces an earlier one with a fresh motive: the city was doomed and the innocent should not share her ruin.
The disputed preposition means at the price of her guilt, not in it or through it, since Israel must flee to save his life and not atone for Babylon.

outliers.claim: Gives a literal rendering of the archer clause that keeps the play the English loses: at him who bends let the bender bend his bow, and at him who glories in his coat of mail.

themes: Against him that bendeth let the archer bend his bow, and against him that lifteth himself up in his brigandine: and spare ye not her young men; destroy ye utterly all her host.
Thus the slain shall fall in the land of the Chaldeans, and they that are thrust through in her streets.
For Israel hath not been forsaken, nor Judah of his God, of the Lord of hosts; though their land was filled with sin against the Holy One of Israel.
Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and deliver every man his soul: be not cut off in her iniquity; for this is the time of the Lord’s vengeance; he will render unto her a recompence.

7.pericope_label: Babylon hath been a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, that made all the earth drunken: the nations have drunken of her wine; therefore the nations are mad. Babylon is suddenly fallen and destroyed: howl for her; take balm for her pain, if so be she may be healed. We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed: forsake her, and let us go every one into his own country: for her judgment reacheth unto heaven, and is lifted up even to the skies. The Lord hath brought forth our righteousness: come, and let us declare in Zion the work of the Lord our God.

schools.summary: Note that the figure of the cup is borrowed and then dropped at the fall, since a golden cup does not break; and refuse to let the call to take balm become a shout of triumph.
Give three accounts of the gold and use the verse to answer the objection that God had himself raised the city so high.
Read the cup as the plenitude of punishment and put the announcement of the fall in the mouth of spectators.

debates.question: Who speaks the words about healing Babylon?

positions.position: Either the allies who tried to defend her or the prophets and good people among the exiles who laboured to convince the inhabitants.
Physicians by metaphor, the subject nations and hired soldiers, pleading afterwards that the fault was not theirs.
The mercenary soldiers, whom the prophet personates.
The exiles answering the prophet's appeal, having done what they could in vain.
Those who would have saved her had it been in their power, but could not turn away the judgment of God.

debates.question: Why is the cup golden?

positions.position: From the liquor, or the material, or the contents, idolatry being as poison in a golden cup.
To mark the splendour of the reigning dynasty.
For outward splendour, but the wine in it was poisoned, intoxicating men with wild ambitions and dark idolatries.

outliers.claim: Refuses to let the call to take balm be a shout of triumph: the captives are to try to heal their oppressor, still seeking the peace of the city.

themes: Babylon hath been a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, that made all the earth drunken: the nations have drunken of her wine; therefore the nations are mad.
Babylon is suddenly fallen and destroyed: howl for her; take balm for her pain, if so be she may be healed.
We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed: forsake her, and let us go every one into his own country: for her judgment reacheth unto heaven, and is lifted up even to the skies.
The Lord hath brought forth our righteousness: come, and let us declare in Zion the work of the Lord our God.

11.pericope_label: Make bright the arrows; gather the shields: the Lord hath raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes: for his device is against Babylon, to destroy it; because it is the vengeance of the Lord, the vengeance of his temple. Set up the standard upon the walls of Babylon, make the watch strong, set up the watchmen, prepare the ambushes: for the Lord hath both devised and done that which he spake against the inhabitants of Babylon. O thou that dwellest upon many waters, abundant in treasures, thine end is come, and the measure of thy covetousness. The Lord of hosts hath sworn by himself, saying, Surely I will fill thee with men, as with caterpillers; and they shall lift up a shout against thee.

schools.summary: Prefer sharpen to make bright, insist the shields are filled by the men who carry them, and read the standard as directing an attack rather than a defence.
Canvass the lexical options and settle them, and make the oath's condescension the doctrine: what does not properly belong to God is transferred to him.
Supply the history of the Median and Persian kings and the dimensions of the walls, and make the filling concrete.

debates.question: Is the standard on the walls a summons to defend or to attack?

positions.position: An ironical order to the Babylonians to gather the inhabitants to their bulwarks, since the city has not yet fallen.
Spoken to the Babylonians, rousing them out of their security.
A call to the enemy to invest the city.
The preposition may mean against, which suits the context better; the standards then signal an attack at a chosen point.

debates.question: Who is commanded to make ready?

positions.position: Either the Medes, summoned to arm, or the Babylonians, taunted for preparing armies to no purpose.
The prophet addresses Babylon.

outliers.claim: Brings an inscription of the king himself, boasting that he made water flow all around in an immense dyke of earth and carried an aqueduct across great waters like the depths of the sea.
States the argument the verses make: neither the strong position on the river nor the treasures that paid for the fortifications can avert what God has decreed.

themes: Make bright the arrows; gather the shields: the Lord hath raised up the spirit of the kings of the Medes: for his device is against Babylon, to destroy it; because it is the vengeance of the Lord, the vengeance of his temple.

Set up the standard upon the walls of Babylon, make the watch strong, set up the watchmen, prepare the ambushes: for the Lord hath both devised and done that which he spake against the inhabitants of Babylon.
O thou that dwellest upon many waters, abundant in treasures, thine end is come, and the measure of thy covetousness.
The Lord of hosts hath sworn by himself, saying, Surely I will fill thee with men, as with caterpillers; and they shall lift up a shout against thee.

15.pericope_label: He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heaven by his understanding. When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens; and he causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth: he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures. Every man is brutish by his knowledge; every founder is confounded by the graven image: for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them. They are vanity, the work of errors: in the time of their visitation they shall perish. The portion of Jacob is not like them; for he is the former of all things: and Israel is the rod of his inheritance: the Lord of hosts is his name.

schools.summary: States the logic of the borrowed passage in one line: the omnipotence of the Creator will destroy the idols of Babylon and break the kingdom that rules it.
Marks that the words were used before to another end, and turns the idol polemic on the craftsmen rather than on men's general vanity.
Distributes the three clauses among omnipotence, omniscience and design, and explains the weather by the natural philosophy of his own century.

debates.question: What does the reproach of brutish knowledge mean?

positions.position: A man is brutish for want of real knowledge, and brutish again when he acknowledges that an idol is anything in the world.
Not the general account of men gliding into error by their own wisdom, but the narrower charge that craftsmen are delirious in thinking their art can make gods.

outliers.claim: Answers the natural philosophers directly: they assign causes, but one must come to the original cause, since exhalations are not created by themselves and God is their sole author.
Notes outright that these five verses are transcribed from an earlier chapter of this book.

themes: He hath made the earth by his power, he hath established the world by his wisdom, and hath stretched out the heaven by his understanding.

When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens; and he causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth: he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures.
Every man is brutish by his knowledge; every founder is confounded by the graven image: for his molten image is falsehood, and there is no breath in them.
They are vanity, the work of errors: in the time of their visitation they shall perish.
The portion of Jacob is not like them; for he is the former of all things: and Israel is the rod of his inheritance: the Lord of hosts is his name.

20.pericope_label: Thou art my battle axe and weapons of war: for with thee will I break in pieces the nations, and with thee will I destroy kingdoms; And with thee will I break in pieces the horse and his rider; and with thee will I break in pieces the chariot and his rider; With thee also will I break in pieces man and woman; and with thee will I break in pieces old and young; and with thee will I break in pieces the young man and the maid; I will also break in pieces with thee the shepherd and his flock; and with thee will I break in pieces the husbandman and his yoke of oxen; and with thee will I break in pieces captains and rulers. And I will render unto Babylon and to all the inhabitants of Chaldea all their evil that they have done in Zion in your sight, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Corrects the weapon to a mace, since the axe is late on Assyrian monuments, and judges the conqueror rather than Babylon to be addressed.
Reads the hammer as Babylon herself and answers the objection of her impregnability from the potter and the vessel.
Keeps the verbs in the past and reads the closing conjunction as an adversative that turns the whole passage.

debates.question: Who is the battle-axe?

positions.position: Most likely Babylon and her king, called the hammer of the whole earth before; possibly the Persian, or even the kingdom of Christ.
The reigning king of Babylon, with all the verbs past.
The conqueror, so that the hammer of the whole earth is broken by a mightier weapon; and the tenses should be present.
Babylon was the hammer God employed, and he will hereafter employ a hammer within Babylon itself.

outliers.claim: Faces the difficulty that a prophet elsewhere has God paying the same king wages for his work, and holds both declarations agree, the reward regarding a people not yet humbled while this promise is given peculiarly to the church.
Treats the three verses of the catalogue as one sentence with one sense, that God had used and was still using the Babylonians to destroy many nations.

themes: Thou art my battle axe and weapons of war: for with thee will I break in pieces the nations, and with thee will I destroy kingdoms;
And with thee will I break in pieces the horse and his rider; and with thee will I break in pieces the chariot and his rider;
With thee also will I break in pieces man and woman; and with thee will I break in pieces old and young; and with thee will I break in pieces the young man and the maid;
I will also break in pieces with thee the shepherd and his flock; and with thee will I break in pieces the husbandman and his yoke of oxen; and with thee will I break in pieces captains and rulers.
And I will render unto Babylon and to all the inhabitants of Chaldea all their evil that they have done in Zion in your sight, saith the Lord.

25.pericope_label: Behold, I am against thee, O destroying mountain, saith the Lord, which destroyest all the earth: and I will stretch out mine hand upon thee, and roll thee down from the rocks, and will make thee a burnt mountain. And they shall not take of thee a stone for a corner, nor a stone for foundations; but thou shalt be desolate for ever, saith the Lord. Set ye up a standard in the land, blow the trumpet among the nations, prepare the nations against her, call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz; appoint a captain against her; cause the horses to come up as the rough caterpillers. Prepare against her the nations with the kings of the Medes, the captains thereof, and all the rulers thereof, and all the land of his dominion. And the land shall tremble and sorrow: for every purpose of the Lord shall be performed against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon a desolation without an inhabitant.

schools.summary: Finds the epithet applied elsewhere to the Mount of Corruption and hears in it the charge that false worship was the root of the city's evils; and reads the past tenses as the prophet seeing the event pass before him.
States the geographical difficulty plainly and answers it from the height of the walls, then makes the desolation perpetual.
Reads the mountain as a volcano and works the figure to an extinguished crater whose ejecta will not serve for a corner stone.

debates.question: Why is a city on a plain called a mountain?

positions.position: From the height of the walls and buildings, the historians giving some two hundred feet.
From the walls, towers and hanging gardens, or because monarchies are compared to mountains.
High in greatness and high in its walls, so that at a distance it looked like a rocky mountain.
The word is literally inapplicable and symbolical of sovereignty; the phrase itself is borrowed from a name given to another hill.

debates.question: Are the kings of the Medes plural or singular?

positions.position: Singular, which the phrase his dominion at the end requires, though one kingdom held many provinces under satraps.
The singular pronoun shows kings, captains and rulers all under one sovereign leader.

outliers.claim: Describes the whole scene as already present to the prophet in spirit: the earth quaking, the mighty men withdrawing dispirited, the enemy firing the houses and breaking the bars.

themes: Behold, I am against thee, O destroying mountain, saith the Lord, which destroyest all the earth: and I will stretch out mine hand upon thee, and roll thee down from the rocks, and will make thee a burnt mountain.
And they shall not take of thee a stone for a corner, nor a stone for foundations; but thou shalt be desolate for ever, saith the Lord.

Set ye up a standard in the land, blow the trumpet among the nations, prepare the nations against her, call together against her the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz; appoint a captain against her; cause the horses to come up as the rough caterpillers.
Prepare against her the nations with the kings of the Medes, the captains thereof, and all the rulers thereof, and all the land of his dominion.
And the land shall tremble and sorrow: for every purpose of the Lord shall be performed against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon a desolation without an inhabitant.

30.pericope_label: The mighty men of Babylon have forborn to fight, they have remained in their holds: their might hath failed; they became as women: they have burned her dwellingplaces; her bars are broken. One post shall run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to shew the king of Babylon that his city is taken at one end, And that the passages are stopped, and the reeds they have burned with fire, and the men of war are affrighted.

schools.summary: Rejects the rendering fords, since the river was not fordable at Babylon, and identifies the crossing-places as bridges and ferries.
Reconstructs the capture from the heathen historians, and explains why the Babylonians could not believe the walls would be passed.
Confesses defeat on the burnt reeds and reports another scholar's conjecture, noting no historian mentions it.

debates.question: What are the burnt reeds?

positions.position: Possibly the marsh reeds fired after the capture to clear the ground, though the sense is uncertain and no historian mentions it.
The word is elsewhere translated pool and probably refers to a great artificial pool.
Vast tall growth along the bank which with the mud served as another wall until the invaders burned it.
Metaphor: the fords were dried as though one had set fire to wood, which suits water not at all and so expresses the miracle more fully.

debates.question: What are the stopped passages?

positions.position: The gates leading from the river to the city, left open that night and now held by soldiers.
The ferries by which one part of the city communicated with the other, with a bridge in the middle and a tunnel beneath.

outliers.claim: Gives the whole stratagem from the heathen authors: two eunuchs of the king, one whose son the tyrant had killed and one castrated by way of disgrace, went over to the besieger and taught him how the city could be taken.

themes: The mighty men of Babylon have forborn to fight, they have remained in their holds: their might hath failed; they became as women: they have burned her dwellingplaces; her bars are broken.
One post shall run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to shew the king of Babylon that his city is taken at one end,
And that the passages are stopped, and the reeds they have burned with fire, and the men of war are affrighted.

33.pericope_label: For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; The daughter of Babylon is like a threshingfloor, it is time to thresh her: yet a little while, and the time of her harvest shall come. Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon hath devoured me, he hath crushed me, he hath made me an empty vessel, he hath swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my delicates, he hath cast me out. The violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon, shall the inhabitant of Zion say; and my blood upon the inhabitants of Chaldea, shall Jerusalem say.

schools.summary: Corrects the threshing-floor to the time when it is trodden and resolves her harvest as the crop the conquerors reap; and names the ground of judgment as Babylon's offences against Israel.
Rejects the received sense of the floor for another drawn from the practice, and works the verbs of the complaint one by one.
Reverses the roles of instrument and floor, and hears a promise inside the complaint that the swallower shall vomit all up.

debates.question: What does the threshing-floor figure mean?

positions.position: The floor in the time when it is trodden; the heaped treasures are the harvest her conquerors reap.
A floor serves only at harvest and is shut up the rest of the year; the city had long been a closed floor without treading, and God declares it will now be used.
The city had been the instrument and the floor on which God threshed other nations, and now becomes the floor where the Chaldeans are threshed.
The wheel has gone over her and she is trodden underfoot.

outliers.claim: Turns the plea for retribution into a lesson, that in extreme evils we should unburden our anxieties in God's bosom rather than murmur and champ the bridle.
Notes that one form of the text has the pronouns plural throughout, and takes the swallowing creature for a crocodile or sea-monster.

themes: For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; The daughter of Babylon is like a threshingfloor, it is time to thresh her: yet a little while, and the time of her harvest shall come.

Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon hath devoured me, he hath crushed me, he hath made me an empty vessel, he hath swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my delicates, he hath cast me out.
The violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon, shall the inhabitant of Zion say; and my blood upon the inhabitants of Chaldea, shall Jerusalem say.

36.pericope_label: Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will plead thy cause, and take vengeance for thee; and I will dry up her sea, and make her springs dry. And Babylon shall become heaps, a dwellingplace for dragons, an astonishment, and an hissing, without an inhabitant. They shall roar together like lions: they shall yell as lions’ whelps. In their heat I will make their feasts, and I will make them drunken, that they may rejoice, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the Lord. I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with he goats.

schools.summary: Lays out the whole range of readings for the drying of the sea, and observes that the mounds of brickwork on the site are now yielding their records to explorers.
Reports three Jewish constructions of the feast in their heat, and makes the prophet's exactness proof that no mortal could have foretold it.
Reads the drying as the exhausting of her treasures and fixes the feast as one held in honour of the city's god.

debates.question: Who roars like lions?

positions.position: Not the invaders, whose capture was silent, but the Chaldeans, revelling at the feast or raging before battle.
Not a continuation of the ruin, but the revelry before the capture, the princes roaring over their prey.
An anticipated objection: though they were lions, their roaring would avail nothing.
The Babylonians, upon the taking of their city.

outliers.claim: Turns the precision of the prediction into evidence: the prophet showed the judgment as by a finger, since no mortal endowed a hundred times with the spirit of divination could have expressed so clearly a thing unknown.
Names the intended effect of the whole passage: the fearful destruction of this city will astonish the world.

themes: Therefore thus saith the Lord; Behold, I will plead thy cause, and take vengeance for thee; and I will dry up her sea, and make her springs dry.
And Babylon shall become heaps, a dwellingplace for dragons, an astonishment, and an hissing, without an inhabitant.
They shall roar together like lions: they shall yell as lions’ whelps.
In their heat I will make their feasts, and I will make them drunken, that they may rejoice, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the Lord.
I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with he goats.

41.pericope_label: How is Sheshach taken! and how is the praise of the whole earth surprised! how is Babylon become an astonishment among the nations! The sea is come up upon Babylon: she is covered with the multitude of the waves thereof. Her cities are a desolation, a dry land, and a wilderness, a land wherein no man dwelleth, neither doth any son of man pass thereby.

schools.summary: Explains the cipher name as balancing the actual name in the parallelism, and rejects the literal flooding of the river on the ground that the cities are to be left arid.
Rejects an alternative identification of the city and makes the prophet's exclamation a device for meeting the hearers' disbelief.
Guesses the city is called by the name of its idol, and lists the wonders that made it the praise of the whole earth.

debates.question: Is the sea that covers Babylon literal water or an army?

positions.position: A figure familiar from an earlier prophet: the city covered by a great sea of nations, the literal reading being clearly inadmissible.
Even the Chaldee paraphrasts took it figuratively, and the very reason the city is covered is that her cities become an arid steppe.
A vast army comparable to the sea for multitude.
A deluge rather than an army, since it was incredible the place could be subdued by the forces of men.

outliers.claim: Finds the prophet dwelling with stern delight on the paradox that the sea overflowing her leaves her cities drier and sandier than before.
Reduces the whole figure to three words, a multitude of enemies.

themes: How is Sheshach taken! and how is the praise of the whole earth surprised! how is Babylon become an astonishment among the nations!
The sea is come up upon Babylon: she is covered with the multitude of the waves thereof.
Her cities are a desolation, a dry land, and a wilderness, a land wherein no man dwelleth, neither doth any son of man pass thereby.

44.pericope_label: And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed up: and the nations shall not flow together any more unto him: yea, the wall of Babylon shall fall. My people, go ye out of the midst of her, and deliver ye every man his soul from the fierce anger of the Lord.

schools.summary: Widens the god's disgorged prey to all the spoil and the nations themselves, and explains why the wall is named here by the inscriptions that consecrate it to him.
Dates the summons to come out after the proclamation of liberty, and cautions that God is not properly incensed against a dead figure.
Identifies the swallowed vessels and reduces the wall to something that will moulder away until it is not discernible.

debates.question: What is the god made to disgorge?

positions.position: The sacred vessels taken from Jerusalem and dedicated in his temple.
Not the vessels and offerings only but all the property Babylon took as spoil, and the nations themselves with life and property.
The vessels and whatever gifts the Babylonians had presented.

debates.question: When is the summons to come out to be obeyed?

positions.position: Not before the capture but after it, when the conqueror proclaimed liberty to return, since the city was destroyed only by a later king.
The anger aimed at Babylon would fall also on those who chose to stay and become partakers of her plagues.
The exhortation also served to raise the hope of a deliverance they thought incredible, lest they remain inebriated with Chaldean indulgences.

outliers.claim: Cautions that God has no quarrel with a dead figure void of reason and feeling, and speaks of the idol as an enemy only for the sake of men.

themes: And I will punish Bel in Babylon, and I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed up: and the nations shall not flow together any more unto him: yea, the wall of Babylon shall fall.
My people, go ye out of the midst of her, and deliver ye every man his soul from the fierce anger of the Lord.

46.pericope_label: And lest your heart faint, and ye fear for the rumour that shall be heard in the land; a rumour shall both come one year, and after that in another year shall come a rumour, and violence in the land, ruler against ruler. Therefore, behold, the days come, that I will do judgment upon the graven images of Babylon: and her whole land shall be confounded, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her. Then the heaven and the earth, and all that is therein, shall sing for Babylon: for the spoilers shall come unto her from the north, saith the Lord. As Babylon hath caused the slain of Israel to fall, so at Babylon shall fall the slain of all the earth. Ye that have escaped the sword, go away, stand not still: remember the Lord afar off, and let Jerusalem come into your mind.

schools.summary: Supplies the actual dynastic news behind the rumours, insists the connecting word has its full force, and calls the closing verses the final summing up of offence and punishment.
Explains why the exiles feared, and refuses to let the personification of heaven and earth be softened into angels and men.
Dates the rumour to the year before the capture and restricts the slain of all the earth to the Chaldeans gathered from all parts.

debates.question: How far do the slain of all the earth extend?

positions.position: Other nations mingled with her people are involved, though perhaps the slain of all the land is the better reading.
They fall throughout her own land, as she had slain Israel.
In a restrained sense, the Chaldeans coming from all parts to help the city being slain there.

debates.question: Who sings at the fall?

positions.position: The whole creation, following an earlier prophet, rejoicing at the judgment and the people's liberation.
A personification including the stars, trees, fishes, birds, fields, stones and rivers; the refined reading of angels and men is frigid.
All the creatures shall rejoice.
The fall is a subject of universal rejoicing.

outliers.claim: Explains the exiles' particular fear, that having had peace in the city's peace they expected to suffer in its calamities.

themes: And lest your heart faint, and ye fear for the rumour that shall be heard in the land; a rumour shall both come one year, and after that in another year shall come a rumour, and violence in the land, ruler against ruler.
Therefore, behold, the days come, that I will do judgment upon the graven images of Babylon: and her whole land shall be confounded, and all her slain shall fall in the midst of her.
Then the heaven and the earth, and all that is therein, shall sing for Babylon: for the spoilers shall come unto her from the north, saith the Lord.
As Babylon hath caused the slain of Israel to fall, so at Babylon shall fall the slain of all the earth.
Ye that have escaped the sword, go away, stand not still: remember the Lord afar off, and let Jerusalem come into your mind.

51.pericope_label: We are confounded, because we have heard reproach: shame hath covered our faces: for strangers are come into the sanctuaries of the Lord’s house. Wherefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will do judgment upon her graven images: and through all her land the wounded shall groan. Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify the height of her strength, yet from me shall spoilers come unto her, saith the Lord. A sound of a cry cometh from Babylon, and great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans: Because the Lord hath spoiled Babylon, and destroyed out of her the great voice; when her waves do roar like great waters, a noise of their voice is uttered:

schools.summary: Makes the confession the exiles' own answer to the prophet, gives the range of reported wall heights, and glosses the great voice as the tumult of life in the streets.
Prefers to read the confession as anticipation, and turns the fortifications into a rule about not measuring God's power by our thoughts.
Reads the shame as reproach cast at their God, and is exact about how far into the sanctuary the plunderers came.

debates.question: Whose words are the confession of shame?

positions.position: The exiles' answer, cast down by the disgrace fallen on them and on the holy city.
The Jews objecting to their return or lamenting the desolation, unable to face a land lying waste.
Anticipation, the prophet repeating what the exiles already said, rather than a formula given them to prepare for return.
The lamentation of the pious for the profanation of the temple.

debates.question: What is the great voice that is destroyed?

positions.position: The city's pride and insufferable boasting.
The noise of multitudes trafficking together.
The stir and tumult of life surging through the streets.
Properly the loud voice, the bustle of the city, the waves being the surging masses of the conquering army.

outliers.claim: Makes the fortifications a rule for reading promises: nothing hinders us more from embracing them than considering what may be done naturally, since consulting our own thoughts excludes a power superior to all means.

themes: We are confounded, because we have heard reproach: shame hath covered our faces: for strangers are come into the sanctuaries of the Lord’s house.
Wherefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will do judgment upon her graven images: and through all her land the wounded shall groan.
Though Babylon should mount up to heaven, and though she should fortify the height of her strength, yet from me shall spoilers come unto her, saith the Lord.
A sound of a cry cometh from Babylon, and great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans:

56.pericope_label: Because the spoiler is come upon her, even upon Babylon, and her mighty men are taken, every one of their bows is broken: for the Lord God of recompences shall surely requite. And I will make drunk her princes, and her wise men, her captains, and her rulers, and her mighty men: and they shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the King, whose name is the Lord of hosts. Thus saith the Lord of hosts; The broad walls of Babylon shall be utterly broken, and her high gates shall be burned with fire; and the people shall labour in vain, and the folk in the fire, and they shall be weary.

schools.summary: Finds a new majesty in the divine name of recompences, and quotes the king's own inscription about the brass folding-doors of the great gates.
Notices that the word just used of God is transferred to the Medes and Persians, and explains the eulogy attached to the divine name.
Quotes the historian who saw the walls and gives their measurements, and reads the drunkenness as the posture of the king and his lords at the feast.

debates.question: What does making the princes drunk mean?

positions.position: The wine of divine wrath, that is, their slaughter, with an allusion to the actual feast.
A plain allusion to the posture of the king and his lords drinking from the temple vessels.
Imagery repeated from a few verses back, carrying forward a thought from an earlier chapter.
An allusion to the feast during which the city was taken, through treachery as well as valour.

outliers.claim: Notes that the clause about labouring in vain is all but verbally identical, and in some manuscripts absolutely so, with a verse in one of the minor prophets.
Observes that without the stratagem the besieger could not humanly have taken a city walled fifty cubits broad and two hundred high.

themes: Because the spoiler is come upon her, even upon Babylon, and her mighty men are taken, every one of their bows is broken: for the Lord God of recompences shall surely requite.

And I will make drunk her princes, and her wise men, her captains, and her rulers, and her mighty men: and they shall sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake, saith the King, whose name is the Lord of hosts.

Thus saith the Lord of hosts; The broad walls of Babylon shall be utterly broken, and her high gates shall be burned with fire; and the people shall labour in vain, and the folk in the fire, and they shall be weary.

59.pericope_label: The word which Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, when he went with Zedekiah the king of Judah into Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. And this Seraiah was a quiet prince. So Jeremiah wrote in a book all the evil that should come upon Babylon, even all these words that are written against Babylon.

schools.summary: Identifies the messenger as the brother of the prophet's own secretary and corrects his title to prince of the resting-place, an office like a quartermaster-general.
Calls the epilogue a sealing of the whole and measures the courage the errand required, while rejecting a rabbinic embellishment of it.
Connects the errand to the message sent to the captives and draws out the sixty years between prophecy and fulfilment.
Reads a character out of the messenger's title and observes what is gained for the word of God by being written and copied.

debates.question: What does the messenger's title mean?

positions.position: Prince of the resting-place, an office like a quartermaster-general, the received rendering being taken from a reformer.
The Syriac made him chief of the camp.
A prince of rest, that is, a man of calm temper who studied the things that make for peace and was no persecutor of the prophets.
A reference to his gentleness and meekness, over which interpreters have toiled needlessly.

debates.question: What was written, and how much of it?

positions.position: Probably no more than the last few verses, the Hebrew word meaning any writing great or small.
A parchment roll, and stress is laid on the whole prophecy standing on one roll, the fitter symbol of the single city.
The prophet wrote it himself, his amanuensis not being with him.

outliers.claim: Fixes the chronology: the fourth year was seven years before Jerusalem was taken, so the prophecy stood above sixty years before its first fulfilment.
Rejects as groundless the Jewish story that the king himself went to Babylon, taken from a book full of fables, and notes the particle will as easily bear from as with.

themes: The word which Jeremiah the prophet commanded Seraiah the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, when he went with Zedekiah the king of Judah into Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. And this Seraiah was a quiet prince.
So Jeremiah wrote in a book all the evil that should come upon Babylon, even all these words that are written against Babylon.

61.pericope_label: And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, When thou comest to Babylon, and shalt see, and shalt read all these words; Then shalt thou say, O Lord, thou hast spoken against this place, to cut it off, that none shall remain in it, neither man nor beast, but that it shall be desolate for ever. And it shall be, when thou hast made an end of reading this book, that thou shalt bind a stone to it, and cast it into the midst of Euphrates: And thou shalt say, Thus shall Babylon sink, and shall not rise from the evil that I will bring upon her: and they shall be weary. Thus far are the words of Jeremiah.

schools.summary: Corrects the opening to see to it and read, calls the reading aloud to a chosen few, and identifies the last sentence as an editorial note by the compiler.
Argues from the address to God that the reading was private, and builds a general account of how the prophetic books were assembled.
Supplies a pagan parallel to the sunken roll and defines which words are meant by the closing note.

debates.question: To whom was the roll read?

positions.position: To a chosen few of his own countrymen; that it was read to the Babylonians is improbable in the highest degree.
Probably to the Jews who were in Babylon.
In a chamber or secret place, since the messenger is bidden to address his words to God and did not undertake the office of a preacher.

debates.question: What is the force of the closing note?

positions.position: An editorial note by whoever compiled the prophecies, telling readers that the narrative following was not written by the prophet.
The prophetical words are meant, since the next chapter is historical and the book of lamentations is not prophecy.
The scribes collected the summaries affixed to the temple doors and added this conclusion, which is not to be confined to the prophecies about this city.

outliers.claim: Supplies a pagan parallel to the sunken roll: a people resolving to leave their country for ever threw a mass of iron into the sea and swore not to return until it should rise and float.

themes: And Jeremiah said to Seraiah, When thou comest to Babylon, and shalt see, and shalt read all these words;
